Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot, and it fixes nearly every weakness I raised there. It randomises with a control group, measures output from administrative records rather than manager ratings, records actual hours from timesheets, and stratifies by type of work. Its results also match what the Halden critique predicted: per-hour gains shrink once you use actual hours, and coverage-bound work loses output. The arithmetic checks out. The remaining issues are mostly about inference with few clusters, gaps in what's reported, and one calculation that strengthens the meetings finding considerably.

## 1. The arithmetic checks out

- **Actual hours.** 33.0 / 37.9 is a 12.9% fall and 31.2 / 37.6 is a 17.0% fall, matching −13% and −17%.
- **Output per actual hour.** 0.979 / 0.87 = +12.5% for case-processing, and 0.886 / 0.83 = +6.7% for counters.
- **Scheduled-hours comparison.** 0.979 / 0.8 = +22%.
- **Strata.** 14 + 10 = 24 offices, and 7 + 5 = 12 treated.

## 2. The meetings data may explain most of the per-hour gain

Combining the timesheet and calendar figures for case-processing offices:

| | Treated | Control |
|---|---|---|
| Actual hours per week | 33.0 | 37.9 |
| Recurring meetings | 3.8 | 7.1 |
| Non-meeting hours | 29.2 | 30.8 |

- Treated staff had only about 5% fewer non-meeting hours than control (29.2 / 30.8 = 0.948).
- Output per FTE fell 2.1%, so output per non-meeting hour rose only about 3% (0.979 / 0.948 = 1.033).
- On these figures, most of the 12.5% gain is accounted for by time moved out of meetings and into casework. That is more than "a substantial part," as the authors put it.

Caveats:

- Meetings were measured only in month six, with no pre-period. The calculation assumes treated and control offices had similar meeting loads at baseline, which randomisation doesn't guarantee with seven offices per arm.
- It also assumes the control offices' month-six meeting level is typical.

This is still worth reporting. It makes the confirmatory test at 24 months more important, and it has a policy implication: much of the gain might be available without cutting hours at all.

**The correlation is weaker than it looks.** With r = 0.71 across 7 offices, t ≈ 2.26 on 5 degrees of freedom, so p ≈ 0.07 two-sided. The 95% confidence interval runs from roughly zero to about 0.95. The authors' own caveats are appropriate, and stating the p-value or interval would make the weakness explicit.

## 3. Inference with 10–14 clusters

Standard cluster-robust standard errors are biased downward with this few clusters, and the counter stratum has only 10 (5 v 5). The reported intervals are probably too narrow. The analysis should use a small-sample correction, such as CR2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom or a wild cluster bootstrap, or randomisation inference. The paper should say which method it used.

Two consequences follow:

- The counter per-hour gain of +6.7% (CI +0.4 to +13.3) may not survive a correction.
- In case-processing, "statistically indistinguishable from control" is not the same as no loss. The interval still includes a loss of nearly 7%. "Little or no measurable loss" in the Discussion should say this, or the paper should report an equivalence test against a pre-specified margin.

## 4. Spillover between offices

Randomising by office prevents contamination between colleagues, but not between workloads.

- **Counter and contact centres.** Contacts handled fell 11.4%. Rising abandonment (6% to 10% of calls) explains only about 4 points of that. Where did the rest of the demand go?
  - If telephone overflow is pooled, or residents switch to another counter office, displaced demand lands in control offices. That raises control output and exaggerates the difference between arms.
  - The paper should describe how calls and visitors are routed, and report control offices' incoming volume.
- **Case-processing.** If cases are allocated from a county-wide queue, the same question applies to case allocation.

## 5. Outcomes reported inconsistently with the registered analysis

The registered analysis is difference-in-differences with confidence intervals, but several rows of Table 1 aren't reported that way:

| Outcome | How it is reported | What is missing |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting time (4.2 → 6.9 min) | Before/after, treated offices only | Control trend and a DiD estimate. It is a registered secondary outcome. |
| Abandoned calls (6% → 10%) | Before/after, treated offices only | Control comparison |
| Appeal overturn rate (3.1% v 3.0%) and repeat contacts (11.8% v 10.9%) | Two numbers | Which arm is which, whether these are levels or DiD, and intervals |
| Sick days (−29%) | Point estimate | Interval |
| Resignations (3.9% v 7.4%) | Raw levels | DiD against the pre-period, and an interval |

**Repeat contacts affect the output measure itself.** If 11.8% is the treated figure, a larger share of counted contacts in treated offices were repeats. "Contacts handled" then overstates the service actually delivered, and the true fall in output is somewhat larger than 11.4%.

**Appeal lag.** Appeals follow decisions with a delay. Overturn rates at nine months may not yet reflect decisions made late in the trial.

## 6. Gaps in measurement and cost

**Backlog in case-processing.** Case-processing has no equivalent of the counter offices' waiting time. With output down about 2% and intake unchanged, backlogs would grow. The paper should report backlog size and time to decision, especially since the Limitations mention statutory deadlines.

**Overtime is a cost.** Case-processing staff worked about 3 hours a week of claimed overtime to clear backlogs. So output per employee was held near control partly by paying extra on top of full pay. The Discussion's point about whether "the hours reduction pays for itself" needs labour cost per unit of output, including overtime, alongside per-hour and per-employee figures.

**Unclaimed hours.** Timesheets capture only overtime that was claimed. Unrecorded work, such as checking email on the day off, would mean actual hours fell less than measured, and the per-hour gain would be overstated. The paper rightly criticises scheduled-hours estimates, and the same logic applies one level down. A brief limitation would cover it.

**Counter offices could have hired.** The trial kept staffing fixed during unchanged opening hours, so lower coverage was designed in. A short estimate of the extra hires needed to maintain waiting times would make the policy trade-off concrete.

## 7. The counter per-hour gain is partly a queueing effect

Counter work responds to demand. With fewer staff present and longer queues, each person spends less time idle between contacts. Some of the +6.7% in output per hour is probably higher utilisation rather than people working better, and the longer waits the public experienced are the other side of the same effect. The Discussion should say so, because it supports the authors' own point that per-hour and per-employee productivity diverge in coverage-bound work.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Define FTE.** Readers need to know whether a treated employee on 30 scheduled hours counts as 1.0 FTE. The paper's figures imply it does (the denominator is headcount), but that should be stated.
- **Control offices' reaction.** Control staff knew about the trial and may have been disappointed by their assignment. That could raise resignations in control and inflate the 3.9% v 7.4% gap. Reporting control resignations against their own pre-period would help.
- **Multiplicity.** There are several secondary outcomes across two strata. A brief note on how they should be read, such as treating them as supportive rather than confirmatory, would help.
- **Staff by stratum.** Report the split of the 1,180 staff between the two strata.

## Overall assessment

The design is sound and the main conclusions follow from the registered analyses. Per-hour gains are overstated when measured against scheduled hours, and coverage-bound work loses output and service quality. The most valuable revisions would be:

1. Small-sample-corrected inference.
2. DiD estimates with intervals for every outcome, including waiting times.
3. A check for demand spillover into control offices.
4. Backlog and cost-per-unit figures, including overtime.
5. The meetings calculation in section 2, which points to an important and possibly larger mechanism than the authors claim.

I can draft a referee report, or write up a short comparison of how this trial's findings bear on the Halden pilot's sector-general claim.
